title: k means clustering
story:
There is no answer to check against here, so the first move is to convert the question into an objective. Fix the number of groups in advance, and define the best grouping as the one minimising the total squared distance from each point to the centre of its group. That done, a procedure suggests itself: assign every point to the nearest centre, recompute each centre as the mean of the points assigned to it, and repeat until nothing moves.

The history is worth a paragraph because it is a clean case of a name and a thing coming apart. MacQueen coined the term k-means in 1967, at the Fifth Berkeley Symposium, and the procedure he proposed updates the centres incrementally as each observation is assigned, needing access to only one data point at a time — an online method. The algorithm almost everyone actually runs is the other one: alternate assignment and recomputation in full batches, written by Lloyd at Bell Telephone Laboratories in 1957 for pulse-code modulation, and not published as a journal article until 1982, twenty-five years later. Forgy published essentially the same method in 1965. So the name comes from one paper and the algorithm from another, and when someone says k-means they almost always mean the thing that was not called that.

Three properties follow directly from the objective and are the whole practical content of the method.

The number of groups is an input. Nothing in the procedure discovers how many groups there are; you assert it, and the assertion is usually the most consequential decision made. Supply a number and you receive that many groups, on structured data and on noise alike.

The objective is not convex, so the procedure finds a local minimum, and which one depends on where the centres started. Two runs from different initialisations give different answers, and neither is wrong in any sense the method can express. The standard response is many restarts, keeping the best by the objective, or a smarter initialisation that spreads the starting centres apart.

And minimising squared distance to a centre encodes an assumption about shape. It prefers groups that are compact and roughly spherical and similar in size, because that is what the criterion rewards. Genuine structure that is elongated, curved or of very unequal density will be cut across rather than found — and since the distances are computed in whatever space your scaling and encoding produced, part of what the method discovers is a consequence of the preprocessing rather than of the data.

problem.name: Centroid-based clustering
problem.shape: Observations need to be grouped by similarity, and there is no label to say which grouping is correct.
tell: a grouping is wanted and no target exists
the number of groups is being chosen by inspection
results differ between runs and someone is treating that as a defect
features were not scaled before distances were computed
problem.move: State the number of groups as the assumption it is, and run from many initialisations, keeping the best by the objective. Scale the features first, because the distances are computed in the space your preprocessing built. Then check stability across resamples, and evaluate against something downstream rather than against the criterion you minimised.
problem.invariant: The procedure minimises total squared distance from points to their assigned centres, decreasing that quantity at every step. It converges to a local minimum of that objective and to nothing else.
problem.breaks: The criterion rewards compact, roughly spherical groups of similar size, so structure that is elongated, curved or of very unequal density is cut across rather than discovered — and the method reports such a partition with exactly the same confidence as a correct one, because the objective was satisfied either way.

cost.time: each pass is linear in points, groups and dimensions, and the number of passes is small — which is why it remains the default despite its assumptions
cost.space: the centres only, so the fitted model is tiny compared with the data
cost.beats: methods that infer the number of groups, which cost far more, and hierarchical approaches, which are quadratic and do not scale

worked.problem: The method gives a different answer on each run. Is that a bug?
worked.reasoning:
No. It is the objective being non-convex, and the behaviour is telling you something you should want to know.

The procedure minimises the total squared distance from each point to its assigned centre. That surface has many local minima, and the algorithm is a descent method: each step — reassign points, recompute centres — cannot increase the objective, so it converges. What it converges to depends on where the centres began. Different initialisations, different basins, different partitions, and every one of them is a genuine local minimum. Nothing has gone wrong.

That it is not a bug does not make it unimportant, though, and there are two quite different things the variation might be telling you.

If the runs differ but the objective values are all similar, the data has several roughly equivalent groupings and the method has no basis for preferring one. That is a fact about the data rather than about the algorithm, and it is worth reporting rather than hiding behind a fixed seed.

If one run reaches a clearly better objective than the others, the poorer runs were simply stuck. That is the ordinary case and it has an ordinary fix.

So in practice: run from many initialisations and keep the one with the best objective, which is what sensible implementations do by default, or use an initialisation scheme that spreads the starting centres apart rather than placing them at random. Fixing the random seed makes the output reproducible and does not make it stable — it conceals the variation instead of addressing it, which matters because the variation is information.

The deeper check is different from either. Resample the data, cluster again, and see whether the same structure reappears. Instability across initialisations on fixed data says the objective has many minima. Instability across resamples says the partition is describing the sample rather than the population, which is the finding that should actually change what you do.

And I would add the thing the question does not ask about: the number of groups was supplied, not discovered, and that assumption is usually more consequential than the initialisation. The method returns exactly as many groups as you asked for, whether or not the data contains any.

problem.practice: Run the method twenty times from random initialisations on the same data and record both the objective and the partition each time. Then do it again on a resample of the data. Compare which kind of instability you have. Finally, scale one feature by a hundred and see how much of the grouping survives.

beats.broke: You want to know which observations belong together and there is no target to check an answer against, so the question must be turned into an objective before it can be answered at all.
beats.fix: Fix the number of groups in advance and minimise the total squared distance from each point to its group's centre, alternating between assigning points to the nearest centre and recomputing the centres.
beats.cost: The objective is not convex, so the result is a local minimum that depends on where it started — and the criterion assumes the structure you want is compact and roughly spherical in whatever space your preprocessing produced.

interview.answer:
No — it is the objective being non-convex, and the variation is telling you something worth knowing.

The procedure minimises total squared distance from points to their assigned centres. That surface has many local minima, and the algorithm is a descent method: each reassign-and-recompute step cannot increase the objective, so it converges, and where it converges depends on where the centres started. Different initialisations land in different basins, and each result is a genuine local minimum.

Not a bug, but not unimportant either, because two different things could be happening. If the runs differ while the objective values are all similar, the data supports several roughly equivalent groupings and the method has no basis for preferring one — a fact about the data, worth reporting rather than hiding. If one run reaches a clearly better objective, the others were simply stuck, which is the ordinary case.

So in practice: many initialisations, keep the best by objective, or use an initialisation that spreads the starting centres apart. Fixing the seed makes the output reproducible without making it stable; it conceals the variation rather than addressing it.

The deeper check is different. Instability across initialisations on fixed data says the objective has many minima. Instability across resamples says the partition describes the sample rather than the population — and that is the finding that should change what you do.

I would also raise what the question skips: the number of groups was supplied rather than discovered, and that assumption usually matters more than the initialisation. The method returns exactly as many groups as you asked for, whether or not the data contains any.

takeaway: The number of groups is asserted rather than discovered and the objective is non-convex, so differing runs are local minima rather than bugs — and squared distance to a centre quietly assumes the structure is compact and round in whatever space your scaling produced.
